paragraphs.text: Heb., With a thick cloud: nothing like that bright cloud wherein he appeared to his people, as a token of his grace, at the dedication of the temple. {1Ki 8:10} How comes it about, and what may be the reason for it? Oh in what a wonderful manner and by what strange means hath the Lord now clouded and covered his people (whom he had established as Mount Zion) with blackest calamities and confusions, taking all the lustre of happiness and of hope from her, and that in his anger, and again in the day of his anger!
paragraphs.anchor: How hath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion witha cloud!

paragraphs.text: “ Tantaene animis coelestibus irae? ”

i.e., From the highest pitch of felicity to the lowest plight of misery. This was afterwards indeed Caperuaum’s case; but when Micah the Morashite prophesied in the times of Jeremiah that "Zion should be ploughed as a field, and Jerusalem laid on heaps," {Mic 3:12 Jer 26:18} it seemed a paradox, and very few believed them. Christ’s disciples also had a conceit that the temple and the world must needs have one and the same period, which occasioned that mixed discourse made by our Saviour. {Mat 24:1-3} But God’s gracious presence is not tied to a place. The ark, God’s footstool (as here it is called) was transportative till settled in Zion; so is the Church militant in continual motion, till it come to triumph in heaven; and those that with Capernaum are lifted up to heaven in the abundance of means, may be brought down to hell for an instance of divine vengeance.
paragraphs.anchor: And cast down from heaven to earth

paragraphs.text: The temple, and therein the ark, to teach them that he was not wholly there included, neither ought now to be sought and worshipped anywhere but above. Sursum corda.
paragraphs.anchor: And remembered not his footstool.

paragraphs.text: Kατεποντισε, {a} as the sea swalloweth up a ship; as an earthquake swalloweth up whole townships; as fire swalloweth up fuel, or as Moses’ serpent swallowed up the sorcerers’ serpents.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord hath swallowed up all the habitations of Jadah.

paragraphs.text: This was worse than all the rest. {Isa 47:6}
paragraphs.anchor: And hath not pitied.

paragraphs.text: Not shaken them only, and so left them standing, but utterly subverted them, and that in great displeasure, Deo irritato, et irato. God set on the Chaldees, and was the author, not of their evil will, but of their work.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath thrown down.

paragraphs.text: Though for their height they seemed to threaten heaven.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath brought them down to the ground.

paragraphs.text: Which were held holy and inviolable. Profanavit regnum coeli, say some Rabbis here, He hath profaned the kingdom of heaven; for so they accounted the commonwealth of Israel, which Josephus calleth Yεοκρατειαν, a God government. But now God had disprivileged them, and cast them off as a thing of naught.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath polluted the kingdom and the priests.

paragraphs.text: {a} Septuag.
i.e., All the strength and beauty, the royal majesty especially. {Psa 89:24; Psa 132:17}
paragraphs.anchor: He hath cut off in his anger all the horn of Israel

paragraphs.text: Wherewith he was wont to shelter them and to fight for them. Or, Israel’s right hand - scil., by disabling them; for it is God that strengtheneth and weakeneth the arm of either party. {Eze 30:24}
paragraphs.anchor: He hath drawn back his right hand.

paragraphs.text: Or, In Jacob - i.e., He declareth his displeasure among his people as clearly as a flame of fire that is easily discerned.
paragraphs.anchor: And he burned against Jacob.

paragraphs.text: He doth not only help the enemies, but himself fighteth against us with his own bare hand. He hath bent his bow, id est, vim suam ultricem, saith Origen; that is, his avenging force. So the poet feigneth that Apollo shot his deadly shafts into the camp of the Grecians.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath bent his bow like an enemy.

paragraphs.text: Heb., He was set. Vulgate, Firmavit dextram suam; he held his right hand steadily, that he might hit what he shot at.
paragraphs.anchor: He stood with his right hand.

paragraphs.text: In Jerusalem, that was sweetly situated, as a tabernacle pitched in a pleasant plain, but now a field of blood.
paragraphs.anchor: In the tabernacle of the daughter of Zion.

paragraphs.text: i.e., Abundantly and most vehemently, perinde ac Aetna, Hecla, &c.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath poured out his wrath like fire

paragraphs.text: This the secure and foolish people would not be drawn to believe, till now they felt it; therefore it is so reiterated.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord was an enemy.

paragraphs.text: This he had said before, {Lam 2:2} but in cases of this kind people love to say the same things over and over. Redundanti copia exponit quae antea dixerat.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath swallowed up Israel, he hath destroyed, &c.

paragraphs.text: And hath increased … mourning and lamentation.] Heb., Lamentation and lamentation - q.d., this is all he hath left us. And this she speaketh mourning, but not murmuring: Non litem intendit Deo, sed confessionem edit.
Redit ad deplorandam religionem: nothing grieves a good soul so much as the loss of religious opportunities. Old Eli’s heart was broken before his neck at the news of the ark taken.
paragraphs.anchor: And he hath violently taken away his tabernacle.

paragraphs.text: As if it were some cottage or hovel set up for a short time in a garden for the repose of the gardener. {Isa 1:8}
paragraphs.anchor: As if it were of a garden.

paragraphs.text: Whence we were wont to hope for help in answer to our prayers. There it was that he formerly "brake the arrows of the bow, the shield, and the sword, and the battle." {Psa 76:3} {See Trapp on "Psa 76:3"} Hence {2Ch 4:9} the great court of the temple, where the people used to pray, is called Gnazarah; that is, help and defence.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath destroyed his places of the assembly.

paragraphs.text: Zedekiah and Seraiah, and with them the kingdom and the priesthood.
paragraphs.anchor: The king and the priest.

paragraphs.text: “ Haec iam pro vill, sub pedibusque iacent. ”

She goeth over it again, as the main matter of her grief, that she was bereft of the outward exercises of religion. His altar God had cast into a corner, as that which was an eyesore to him; his sanctuary he abhorred or dissolved, &c. Longe fecit, procul removit a se quasi rem odiosam, sibi ingratam et molestam.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord hath cast off his altar.

paragraphs.text: Where God was wont to be praised with heart and voice, now the enemies reboate and roar out Io triumphe, Io Paean, Victoria, All is our own.
paragraphs.anchor: They have made a noise in the house of the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Non casu, non subito, non temere, sed maturo el destinato decreto. God’s providence (which is nothing else but the carrying on of his decree) extendeth to smallest matters, much more to the subversion of states and cities.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord hath purposed to destroy.

paragraphs.text: scil., Of destruction, or a levelling line. See 2Ki 21:13 Isa 34:11. Jerusalem was built by line, and so it was destroyed by him who doeth all things in number, weight, and measure.
paragraphs.anchor: He that stretched out a line

paragraphs.text: So they seem to be, because laid on the ground, and covered with rubbish. The Rabbis fable, that the gates sank indeed into the ground, that they might not come into the enemy’s power, because the ark had once passed through them; and when the priests that carried it sang, "Lift up your heads, O ye gates," &c., they opened of their own accord.
paragraphs.anchor: Her gates are sunk into the ground.

paragraphs.text: scil., Read, or regarded. Inter arma silent leges, The noise of wars drowns the voice of laws.
paragraphs.anchor: The law is no more

paragraphs.text: See Psa 74:9. {See Trapp on "Psa 74:9"} Jeremiah was alone, and haply thought, when he saw all ruined, that he should prophesy no more. Ezekiel and Daniel were far remote. This was no small affliction that is here complained of. How woe begone was sinful Saul, when in his distress he could have no answer from God either by Urim or vision, &c., but had the devil to preach his funeral!
paragraphs.anchor: Her prophets also find no vision from the Lord.

paragraphs.text: Who sat once aloft passing sentence, and held themselves, haply, too high to be told their duties by a poor prophet.
paragraphs.anchor: The elders of the daughters of Zion.

paragraphs.text: After the manner of mourners.
paragraphs.anchor: Sit upon the ground.

paragraphs.text: Who were wont to be the oracles of the country.
paragraphs.anchor: And keep silence.

paragraphs.text: Those white heads of theirs, which they had stained with foul practices.
paragraphs.anchor: They have cast dust upon their heads.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Sacks, instead of silks.
paragraphs.anchor: They have girded themselves with sackcloth.

paragraphs.text: Who were wont to walk haughtily, and with outstretched necks. {Isa 3:16}
paragraphs.anchor: The virgins of Jerusalem.

paragraphs.text: As if they were ashamed of themselves, and had small joy of their beauty and former bravery.
paragraphs.anchor: Hang down their heads to the ground.

paragraphs.text: Those fountains (as the Hebrew word signifieth) are even drawn dry. I have wept till I can weep no more, as David did; or I have wept myself blind, as Faustus the son of Vortigern (once king of England) is said to have done.
paragraphs.anchor: Mine eyes do fail with tears.

paragraphs.text: Heb., Bemudded. See Lam 1:20.
paragraphs.anchor: My bowels are troubled.

paragraphs.text: I have well nigh vomited up my gall. {as Job 16:13}
paragraphs.anchor: My liver is poured upon the earth.

paragraphs.text: Heb., The breach even to shivers, as young trees or ships are broken by tempests.
paragraphs.anchor: For the destruction.

paragraphs.text: Miserabile etiam hostibus spectaculum; a rueful sight.
paragraphs.anchor: Because the children and sucklings swoon in the streets.

paragraphs.text: Lege et luge. Gather and mourne.
paragraphs.anchor: They say to their mothers.

paragraphs.text: “ Tu quibus ista leges incertum est, Lector, ocellis:
Ipse quidem siccis scribere vix potui. ”

As oft as I read the Lamentations of Jeremiah, saith Gregory Nazianzen, {a} my voice faileth me, and I am overwhelmed with tears. The misery of that poor people cometh under my view, as it were, and my heart is therewith very much affected and afflicted.

Frumentum dicunt, non panem. They say grain not bread. Grain they would have been glad of, though unground, saith one; wine they ask for, and not water, which noteth an ill custom in their mothers to drink wine, and to give it their little ones; but by grain and wine here may be meant necessary food, to keep them alive.
paragraphs.anchor: Where is corn and wine.

paragraphs.text: When their soul was poured out into the mother’s bosom.] As it were giving them their lives again, seeing they yielded them no food to preserve them alive.
{a} Orat. i. Pacificat.

q.d., Thou art such a mirror of God’s heavy judgments, that I know not whence to borrow arguments, nor where to find examples for thy comfort, so matchless is thy misery. It exceedeth that of the Egyptians under Moses, of the Canaanites under Joshua, of the Philistines under David, of the Hebrews under Eli, &c. It is even imparallel and inexpressible. I have but one simile to set it forth by, and it is this,
paragraphs.anchor: What thing shall I take to witness for thee?

paragraphs.text: As far as the sea exceedeth the rivers, so doth thy calamity exceed that of other nations.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy breach is great, like the sea.

paragraphs.text: None but an almighty Physician. Surely, in man’s judgment, thy bruise is incurable, and thy wound is grievous. {Jer 30:12}
paragraphs.anchor: Who can heal thee?

paragraphs.text: Thine, and not mine; for thou art miserable by thine own election, accessary to thine own ruin.
paragraphs.anchor: Thy prophets.

paragraphs.text: Visions of vanity, sapless and savourless stuff; the fruit, or rather froth, of their own fancies. {Jer 23:9-14}
paragraphs.anchor: Have seen vain and foolish things for thee.

paragraphs.text: Conviction maketh way for conversion, and so preventeth utter subversion.
paragraphs.anchor: And they have not discovered thine iniquity.

paragraphs.text: viz., Against Babylon, in confidence whereof thou hast been hardened and heartened in thy sinful practices, to thine utter undoing.
paragraphs.anchor: But have seen for thee false burdens

paragraphs.text: scil., Eventually, and as it hath proved.
paragraphs.anchor: And causes of banishment

paragraphs.text: See Lam 1:17.
paragraphs.anchor: All that pass by thee clap.

paragraphs.text: God’s palace upon earth, the porch of paradise, &c., as they said of Jezebel when she lay torn with dogs, Is this that Jezebel?
paragraphs.anchor: Is this the city?

paragraphs.text: “ O quantum haec Niobe, Niobe mutatur ab ills? ”
They speak largely and freely to thy dishonour, the very banks of blasphemy being broken down, as it were.
paragraphs.anchor: All thine enemies opened their mouths against thee.

paragraphs.text: But shall find her to be hard meat, such as they shall digest in hell. See Lam 2:2; Lam 2:5.
paragraphs.anchor: We have swallowed her up.

paragraphs.text: Pray we that the Papists may never see here their longlooked for day, as they have long called it.
paragraphs.anchor: Certainly this is the day that we look for.

paragraphs.text: Or, Performed what he purposed. See Lam 2:8.
paragraphs.anchor: The Lord hath done that which he hath devised.

paragraphs.text: That is, his threats annexed to his commands, and of as great authority as they.
paragraphs.anchor: He hath fulfilled his word that he had commanded.

paragraphs.text: And not two or three days only since. God’s menaces are ancient and infallible, not uttered in terrorem only; neither is his forbearance any acquittance.
paragraphs.anchor: In the days of old.

paragraphs.text: Still the prophet calleth off this distressed people from the jeers and insolencies of their enemies, whom they too much looked upon, to the just judgment of God, who turned those dogs loose upon them, to bark at them and to bait them, in the manner said before.
paragraphs.anchor: And he hath caused thine enemy to rejoice over thee.

paragraphs.text: i.e., They cried seriously at least, if not sincerely. Some think it was not a cry of the spirit for grace, but only of the flesh, for ease and freedom from affliction; wherefore the prophet in the next words turneth to the walls of Jerusalem, which were now broken down, bidding them weep, since the people would not. And surely the stony walls of men’s houses, standing with bells of water on their faces before foul weather, shall witness against such hard hearts as relent not, and so prevent not the terrible tempest of God’s wrath for their iniquities.
paragraphs.anchor: Their herd cried unto the Lord

paragraphs.text: There are those who render and sense the text thus: "Their heart crieth against the Lord," - i.e., The adversaries set their whole power to devise blasphemy against God; let the Church therefore pray in hope to be heard, and to speed the better for the other’s insolence. These by wall understand the people within the wall. Others, O mure, qui nunc es mera ruina; O poor shattered wall; or, O city, which art now nothing but bare walls, without housing and inhabitants.
A fit time for meditation and prayer, as we read of David, {Psa 119:55; Psa 119:148} and of the Son of David. {Luk 21:37}
paragraphs.anchor: Arise, cry in the night.

paragraphs.text: . When others are in their first - which is their deepest and sweetest - sleep, break thyself of thy rest, that thou mayest give God no rest. {Isa 62:6-7} Omnibus signis et modis miseriam tuam expone Domino; bestir thee every way, all is but little enough.
paragraphs.anchor: In the beginning of the watches.

paragraphs.text: That is, saith Sanchez, Weep till thou hast wept thy very heart out, if it were possible. Or as others, Pour out thine heart to God in humble and ingenuous confession and supplication; but then pour it forth as water (whereof every drop will come out), and not as oil, whereof some will still stick to the sides of the vessel. Tundens pectus et non effundens vitia, ea consolidat, saith Augustine. He who pretendeth to repent, and yet parteth not with his sins, doth but increase them.
paragraphs.anchor: Pour out thine heart like water.

paragraphs.text: But with thy heart. {Lam 3:41}
paragraphs.anchor: Lift up thine hands toward him.

paragraphs.text: See on Lam 2:11-12.
paragraphs.anchor: For the life of thy young children.

paragraphs.text: Even to thine own inheritances, who suffer harder and heavier things commonly than any others. And why? Ingentia beneficia, ingentia flagitia, ingentia supplicia; their offences are increased, their punishments are aggravated by their obligations.
paragraphs.anchor: Behold, O Lord, and consider to whom thou hast done this.

paragraphs.text: That they did so in the siege of Jerusalem by the Chaldees, it appeareth by this question. In the famine of Samaria, under Joram, they did likewise; {2Ki 6:28-29} as also at the last destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans; {a} and at the siege of Sancerra, in France, A.D. 1572. See the sad effects of sin, and shun it, if but for the ill consequents of it.
paragraphs.anchor: Shall the women eat their fruit, children of a span long?

paragraphs.text: It seems they were so - but who they were we read not - although God had cautioned, "Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm." Priests were slaughtered, where they used to slaughter beasts for sacrifices; but it may be they were nothing better than Thomas Becket, the devil’s martyr, here, and Adam Benton, that butcherly archbishop in Scotland, who, when himself was butchered, cried out, Kill me not, for I am a priest. {b}
paragraphs.anchor: Shall the priest and the prophet be slain in the sanctuary of the Lord?

paragraphs.text: {a} Joseph. de Bel., lib. vii. cap. 8.
{b} Acts and Mon.
Oh, the woe of war! oh, the bloody work that the sword maketh wheresoever it is in commission! Well may it be called "an evil, an only evil," by an antonomasy. {a} {Isa 45:7}
paragraphs.anchor: The young and the old lie on the ground in the streets.

paragraphs.text: {a} The substitution of an epithet or appellative, or the name of an office or dignity, for a person’s proper name, as the Iron Duke for Wellington, his Grace for an archbishop. Also, conversely, the use of a proper name to express a general idea, as in calling an orator a Cicero, a wise judge a Daniel. ŒD

i.e., My terrible enemies the Chaldees, being called in by thee their generalissimo, came on as cheerfully as if they had come to a solemn feast or some merry meeting, and not to a siege and to a bloody war, which they cannot but know to be utrinque triste, such as both sides usually suffer by.
paragraphs.anchor: Thou hast called as in a solemn day my terrors

paragraphs.text: Singula haec verba ponderanda sunt; singula enim ingens habent pathos. Here every word is very ponderous and pathetic; indeed, this whole book is so, which is the reason that there is no great coherence in some places thereof to be discovered. For as he that is under some grievous affliction, without observing of order, now cries, now prays, now laments, now complains, &c.; so doth the prophet here, in the name of the Church, pour forth himself tumultuously in a flood such words as his grief ministered unto him; and grief is no methodical speaker.
paragraphs.anchor: Those that I have swaddled and brought up.
